Q01: Start with actors and three concrete actions, then ask what failure would be unacceptable. Separate required behavior from assumed scale, latency, freshness and availability. State exclusions and one invariant before drawing components. For example, booking may tolerate stale browsing but must serialize the last-seat decision. Explain which answer would change the design; do not invent a global scale requirement just to justify more services.
Q02: Convert active users times actions per user into requests per day, divide by the chosen activity window, and state a separate peak assumption. Estimate mean inflight work as arrival rate times mean time using consistent units. A percentile latency is not automatically a mean for that formula. Distinguish registered users, daily users, sessions, simultaneous clients and requests; they cannot substitute for one another.
Q03: Multiply records per period by retained periods and assumed logical record bytes, then account separately for indexes, replicas, backups and derived artifacts. Estimate bandwidth from request rate and transferred bytes, with reads, writes and cache misses distinguished. Show decimal versus binary units and vary the largest uncertain inputs. The result is planning arithmetic until a real workload measures actual storage and transfer overhead.
Q04: Identify the saturated resource using latency, errors, CPU, memory, I/O, pool and queue evidence. Scaling up can preserve a simple transaction authority until its cost or ceiling matters. Scaling out helps separable work but adds coordination, routing and state distribution. Neither fixes an inefficient query, hot key or slow dependency automatically. Preserve the invariant and define the measurement that would justify the next step.
Q05: Begin with the smallest deployment that gives clear module responsibilities and transaction ownership. A modular monolith often fits a small team and uncertain product boundaries. Separate a service when independent scaling, deployment, ownership or isolation supplies a concrete benefit. Explain the new network, consistency, operational and debugging cost. Package boundaries and deployment boundaries are different; a distributed diagram is not proof of better architecture.
Q06: Group behavior around a state owner and its invariants, then trace who may mutate that state and through which API or transaction. Controllers validate transport, services enforce business policy, and repositories implement scoped persistence. Cross-module reads and events need explicit contracts. Avoid two services independently updating one business entity without an ownership rule, and do not let a convenient shared table silently become every module's public API.
Q07: Use a synchronous call when the caller needs a bounded result now and can accept the dependency. Use durable queued work when accepted execution can finish later, and publish an event when independent consumers react to an occurrence. Specify timeout, acknowledgement, replay and error behavior. Asynchrony shifts latency and failure state rather than removing it; an accepted response needs a truthful completion/status contract.
Q08: A reverse proxy forwards requests; a load balancer selects eligible upstream capacity; an API gateway applies shared edge contracts; a BFF adapts an API/session flow for a particular client. One product can implement several roles. State which hop authenticates identity, what headers it may assert and what the backend revalidates. Naming all four boxes does not justify four deployments or authorize trusting arbitrary incoming identity headers.
Q09: An instance is replaceable when required session, operation and business state survives outside that process or is recoverable under its credential contract. Local caches and temporary work can still exist. Affinity may improve locality, but the selected instance can fail or become hot. Explain recovery after rerouting and distinguish process-local coordination from fleet-wide authority before calling an application stateless.
Q10: List the authoritative writes and required reads, their keys, filters, ordering, cardinality and transaction relationships. Choose indexes and schema around those access patterns, then test plans with representative data. A relational transaction may suit constrained related state; a document model may suit another aggregate boundary. Search, object bytes and analytics projections have separate access needs. Brand familiarity is not an access-pattern argument.
Q11: Reproduce the actual query and bind values, inspect its execution plan and row estimates, and check indexes, sort work, returned rows and lock/pool waits. Separate query execution from network transfer and application serialization. Fix unnecessary work and verify the changed plan/latency before proposing sharding. A tiny local plan proves selected access behavior, not production capacity on a different dataset.
Q12: Replication maintains copies for selected read, recovery or availability needs; it introduces lag and a failover contract. Partitioning divides a dataset, while sharding places partitions across independent storage authorities. Choose a key from access, skew and transaction requirements. More shards do not split every hot key or preserve cross-shard invariants automatically. Explain routing, rebalancing and failure ownership separately from adding replicas.
Q13: Identify the exact decision requiring current authority: last-seat allocation, nonnegative debit or current access may need a transaction or equivalent serialization. Search/feed freshness can be asynchronous under a stated visibility rule. Eventual consistency is not permission to violate an invariant. During a partition, state which operations reject, wait or accept weaker guarantees; CAP does not classify all ordinary latency tradeoffs by itself.
Q14: Cache a measured expensive read with an explicit key, freshness window, capacity and miss policy. Keep canonical state independent if eviction/loss is allowed. Define write invalidation and late-refill handling, not only TTL. Tenant/owner/version dimensions can be correctness requirements in the key. S10 deliberately probes canonical versions on every hit, so its cache mechanism does not eliminate all source traffic.
Q15: Measure request and byte skew rather than just distinct-key distribution. Coalesce same-key misses within a defined scope, stagger expiry/warmup and cap fallback load. A local lock does not coordinate a fleet. Read replication or near-caches may help a hot immutable key; mutable hot state can require another authority/data model. Additional virtual nodes alone do not divide one key's traffic.
Q16: A work queue distributes an execution obligation among competing workers; publish/subscribe gives independent subscribers their own reaction/progress. Retention and replay can be implemented with a log, but do not define effect correctness by themselves. Clarify fanout, consumer identity, order, retry and acknowledgement. Notification delivery, internal jobs and analytics may share primitives while retaining different business completion rules.
Q17: Name the delivery/effect boundary and failure model before using these terms. A delivery can repeat while a local unique receipt and transaction prevent a repeated business effect. At-most-once can lose work; at-least-once requires duplicate-safe effects. An exactly-once claim for one cooperative transaction does not extend to an unrelated payment, email or database. State retention and replay assumptions as part of the guarantee.
Q18: Allocate an end-to-end deadline across dependencies, then choose bounded attempts, per-attempt timeout, backoff/jitter and an error classification. Retries require remaining budget and safe identity, especially after an unknown remote outcome. Avoid retry multiplication across layers. Measure dependency behavior and saturation rather than treating every timeout as a known failure or assuming a longer timeout repairs overload.
Q19: Scope a stable operation ID to the authenticated caller/tenant, bind it to immutable original intent and enforce uniqueness at the effect authority. Commit the receipt and local effect together, then return the stored outcome on equivalent replay. Changed intent conflicts. For a remote payment, retain the same provider operation and reconcile uncertainty; a local receipt written separately cannot make the remote boundary atomic.
Q20: Use a uniqueness constraint for exclusive identity, a conditional update/version for state conflicts, and short transaction locks where a multi-row invariant needs serialization. A lease provides temporary execution ownership and requires stale-writer fencing at the protected resource. These mechanisms solve different races and can be combined. Expiry cannot stop a paused process or make an unrelated downstream write safe.
Q21: The outbox commits business state and durable publication intent together so a lost immediate publish cannot strand accepted work. The publisher can still repeat after losing acknowledgement, so consumers need their own effect identity. Track retries, retention and ordering under the selected contract. It closes a local dual-write gap; it does not make every consumer or external provider part of the original transaction.
Q22: A saga coordinates a sequence of local transactions when one global transaction is unsuitable. Each step needs durable state, identity, retry/reconciliation and a domain-specific compensating action. Compensation can fail or be unable to undo delivered email, consumed service or irreversible external effects. A recorded refund intent is not a completed refund. Explain operator recovery and the difference between rollback and a later corrective action.
Q23: Derive tenant context from a verified session/membership decision, then enforce current action/resource policy in SQL, lists, caches, jobs, files, retrieval and result delivery. A frontend namespace, guessed UUID or valid JWT is not resource permission. Test known foreign identifiers, revoked grants and changed roles across every path. External storage/search adapters need scoped authenticated contracts, not just a tenant field copied from the request body.
Q24: Specify workload, correctness properties, latency/error objectives, freshness and recovery targets, then collect appropriate runtime and failure evidence. Separate availability from a successful health endpoint and throughput from registered users. Report hardware, payload, concurrency, duration, warm/cold state and error rate for performance tests. Local controlled examples and planning arithmetic are useful evidence with limited scope, not global SLO proof.
Q25: Define create/redirect behavior, destination validation, code ownership, expiry and disable. Insert unique random codes with bounded collision retry and retain scoped create intent for client replay. Redirect reads may use cache only within the disable/expiry contract; analytics can be asynchronous and bounded. Estimate read-heavy traffic, avoid fetching arbitrary destinations merely to validate them, and explain public versus private metadata access.
Q26: Choose the quota subject and algorithm from burst/fairness needs, then make shared check-and-update atomic across application instances. Include clock/refill/cost rules, bounded state and a documented degraded policy. Fixed windows, sliding approximations and token buckets have different boundary behavior. A per-process counter cannot enforce one global quota after horizontal scaling, and stale read replicas cannot arbitrate the final token.
Q27: Persist notification intent and eligible delivery fanout, then use bounded claims, attempts, deadlines and shared provider cooldowns. Bind signatures to the documented raw payload and subscription authority. A receiver can commit before its reply is lost, so delivery repeats need receiver-side effect dedupe. Preferences, poison payloads and manual replay are business policies. A worker attempt is not evidence that the user or endpoint received the message.
Q28: Separate owned metadata from immutable object bytes. Bind upload capabilities to scope/version/expiry, validate completion and quarantine untrusted content before ready publication. Commit durable processing intent with accepted metadata; fence stale workers and make cleanup recoverable. Handle object-without-metadata and metadata-without-object gaps. Local file tests do not prove cloud multipart, antivirus or signed-CDN revocation behavior.
Q29: Keep authoritative inventory and active holds under a transaction/constraint that prevents overselling across callers. Define hold expiry from authority time and atomically confirm or release. Browsing may lag; allocation cannot rely solely on a stale cache. Payment is a separate authority, so late success after expiry needs a compensation/reconciliation decision rather than reassigning inventory that another user already acquired.
Q30: Commit messages with stable room/client operation identity before durable acknowledgement. Define room ordering, bounded catchup and reconnect cursors; use live delivery only as a hint unless its contract says otherwise. Revalidate current membership on history and delayed delivery. Distinguish accepted message, device delivery and reported read state. The local chapter uses HTTP polling, while WebSocket connection routing remains an architectural extension.
Q31: Separate canonical owned/versioned posts/media from derived viewer candidate pointers. Use bounded push fanout where useful and eligible pull candidates for high-fanout authors. Commit batch pointers and frontier together, handle new-follow backfill, and recheck current follow/block/delete/media state at read time. Define stable pagination under the chosen chronological/ranked order. A stale pointer is not a retained permission grant.
Q32: Persist stable jobs and recurring occurrence identities, then admit due work with tenant/concurrency limits and temporary claim tokens. Bound renewal, retries and completion deadlines. Commit local effects with unique receipts and reconcile external uncertainty. Specify missed-run/overlap/cancellation policy and recovery backlog. A failed scheduling status can coexist with a committed effect whose acknowledgement was lost.
Q33: Snapshot server-derived order price/currency/entitlement, use stable provider operation identity and preserve unknown outcomes. Converge replies, verified callbacks and reconciliation on one grant transaction. Post balanced integer-unit journals with conditional nonnegative spending and appended reversals. Keep event, payment, order and ledger identities distinct. Application CREDIT arithmetic does not establish bank settlement or external refund completion.
Q34: Choose exact, token full-text, prefix, substring or semantic retrieval from the query contract. Keep canonical document/version/access separate from a rebuildable index with durable update/delete intent. Filter current tenant, version and permission before top-k and any title/snippet/count/suggestion disclosure. Evaluate representative judged queries. The S9 engine is actual SQLite FTS5; its token-prefix mode is not arbitrary substring completion.
Q35: Separate backend admission from key placement and source value authority. A stable virtual-node ring chooses distinct physical copies, while health/drain controls eligibility. Bound memory, miss fallback and stale-fill behavior across updates, epochs and node incarnations. Rejoin cold or complete a documented resynchronization. Measure hot-key request skew separately from key counts; the local model does not execute a network proxy or replication protocol.
Q36: Model global users separately from current tenant memberships, with an explicit role/owner/share action matrix. Bind sessions to verified active context and rotate on checked tenant switch. Make invitation recipient/audience/role/expiry/revocation and one-time effects explicit. Admit quotas atomically and recheck delayed work/delivery. Keep browser/BFF, SQL, files and retrieval trust boundaries distinct and exercise foreign-ID tests.
Q37: Version canonical text, parsing/chunking and embedding/index profiles. Commit durable ingest intent and fence stale publication. Retrieve only current authorized evidence, bind exact supplied chunks to one generation request, reserve bounded usage and validate citations/tools/current sources before acceptance. Recheck delivery and track deletion across retained projections/context. Feature-hash/extractive fixtures establish orchestration mechanics, not real-model semantic or factual quality.
Q38: Persist scoped immutable occurrence IDs and explicit event/receipt times. Process bounded ordered source batches with projection effects and progress atomically. Publish a versioned metric definition, cohort denominator, freshness and late-data policy. Rebuild from retained canonical decisions and handle subject erasure/replay. A dashboard's plausible chart is not proof of complete ingestion, a correct cohort or causal product impact.
Q39: Let the authoritative unique constraint decide the collision. Retry generation under a bound for a new random code; do not overwrite an existing owner's mapping. Separately retain the creator's operation identity so equivalent client replay returns its original code. Race independent callers and inspect stored uniqueness. Probabilistic rarity does not eliminate the need for a collision path.
Q40: Both servers must arbitrate at one shared atomic quota authority. Read-check-write in separate operations permits two winners. Use a conditional update or atomic script/transaction implementing the chosen algorithm and subject key. Test the exact final-token race on independent callers, clock/cost bounds and degraded behavior. A local process lock or asynchronous replica read does not provide the required shared decision.
Q41: The sender cannot infer nonacceptance from a lost reply. Retry the same delivery identity within budget and verify that the receiver atomically dedupes the event with its business effect. A signature authenticates the payload but does not prevent repeated effects by itself. Record durable attempts and eventual outcome; the notification chapter exercises actual local connection loss after receiver commit.
Q42: Inspect metadata, exact object/version and durable processing intent rather than trusting one callback. Equivalent completion must converge on one accepted version/job. Fence delayed worker publication after delete/expiry/replacement, and reconcile orphan artifacts created before metadata rollback. Keep quarantine and cleanup state explicit. Actual cloud upload notifications and processing services require additional integration evidence.
Q43: Serialize the final-seat hold at inventory authority, then evaluate current hold expiry when confirming. Only one contender can acquire the scarce unit. If payment succeeds after the hold has expired and inventory moved elsewhere, preserve the charge evidence and initiate the chosen refund/review path without overselling. A compensation record is not provider refund execution; reconciliation must resolve that separate boundary.
Q44: Use a stable client message operation scoped to sender/room and return the same committed message on replay. A lost sender acknowledgement may follow a durable append. Recover history from a bounded room sequence/cursor rather than treating live hints as the only copy. Revalidate current membership and distinguish send acceptance from receiver delivery/read claims.
Q45: Estimate fanout amplification and active-reader skew, then consider pull-on-read or hybrid treatment for hot authors. Bound push batches and persist progress with unique pointers. A mode change needs defined semantics for old posts/backfill. Final reads still enforce current graph, block, post and media visibility; avoiding fanout writes does not remove merge cost or privacy obligations.
Q46: After lease expiry, the new worker may reclaim the same logical job. Its effect authority must recognize an existing committed receipt and avoid repeating the effect, then acknowledge. Fence the old token too. The local counter receipt and increment share a transaction; a remote effect requires downstream idempotency/lookup rather than a queue-side receipt alone.
Q47: Return or retain an uncertain/pending state unless authoritative evidence establishes success/failure. Reuse the original provider request identity and reconcile the same order/payment. Do not invent a new charge key merely because transport failed. Verified success grants once across callbacks and synchronous replies, while a second distinct payment becomes an explicit unexpected-charge review case.
Q48: Treat stale index rows as candidates and consult current canonical tenant/access/deletion/version state before exposing any result. Suggestions, snippets and counts also disclose content. A retained tombstone/watermark prevents old upsert resurrection. Define temporary false negatives during edit lag and cache/download revocation boundaries; an already delivered page cannot be retrospectively erased by a later permission check.
Q49: Health can remove a node from eligibility without changing configured placement. On rejoin, discard old cache contents or finish a documented resynchronization before serving. Fence old fills by source version, membership epoch and incarnation where appropriate. Bound fallback/warmup and inspect hot-key load. The local model verifies controlled state changes, not failure detection or distributed membership agreement.
Q50: Derive active tenant from verified context, query the requested object within that scope and enforce current action/owner/share policy. A valid session, known UUID or UI restriction is insufficient. Apply the same rule to lists, writes, exports and workers. Test known foreign IDs, demotion, removed membership and result delivery after revocation; document whether denial returns 403 or hides existence with 404.
Q51: Bind worker payloads/chunks to immutable source version and index profile, then check current canonical state before publication. Scope retrieval to verified tenant and current permission/version before ranking. Bind citations to the exact supplied request evidence and recheck acceptance/delivery. Old embeddings may remain physically present temporarily but must not authorize a current answer or cross-tenant disclosure.
Q52: Replay the same occurrence identity without adding another projection effect. For a distinct late event, apply the declared mutable-window or restatement policy; retain exclusions explicitly. Commit count/cohort changes with progress and define the metric's population. Rebuild must preserve or intentionally version historical inclusion decisions, rather than applying today's watermark to all old events and silently changing history.
Q53: Explain stable ring lookup, virtual points, distinct physical copies and measured primary/copy-set movement over the same key sample. Separate placement from live request balancing and hot-key traffic. Report hardware/workload/concurrency/duration/errors for any actual performance result. The new local sample is independent teaching evidence, not proof of an original resume benchmark; unresolved original claims remain unresolved.
Q54: Trace browser credential, BFF validation, authenticated backend hop and backend resource authorization separately. Verify the actual documented session/JWE implementation before naming it as project fact. Encryption or a signed token does not establish current tenant membership by itself. Reject spoofable identity headers, keep secrets out of the client, and explain browser cookie/CSRF controls without claiming the local bearer fixture implemented them.
Q55: Choose a signed capability or high-entropy opaque token with verified recipient/audience/tenant/scope/expiry. Keep mutable revocation and one-time acceptance effects at a durable authority. Limit issuance/acceptance abuse by appropriate scoped budgets and permissions. A consumed invite must not restore later-removed membership. The executed S11 alternative is opaque server state; signed-token and email-delivery behavior are architectural extensions.
Q56: Specify complete input schemas, stable external row/occurrence matching, explicit timezone conversion and supported nested structures. Commit bounded updates with progress, retry equivalent batches and reconcile partial source snapshots. Reject unsupported records instead of silently flattening away fields. Separate connector, canonical event and analytical projection checkpoints. The local event API demonstrates transaction/time principles without executing an external spreadsheet connector.
Q57: Define business calendar, holidays, timezone/DST, task transitions and escalation tiers before scheduling scans. Give each logical alert a stable task/tier/threshold identity, persist state/outbox and retry delivery safely. Recompute deadlines under an explicit calendar/version policy and audit changes. A cron schedule alone neither calculates working-day deadlines nor proves an escalation message reached its recipient.
Q58: Normalize provider usage by model/version, units and pricing version, then use exact arithmetic and a durable reservation/settlement ledger. Define failed/unknown call policy and retain stable request/provider identity across retries. Settle once when trusted usage arrives and reconcile unresolved reservations. S12 uses character-budget fixtures, while S8 demonstrates CREDIT journals; neither is evidence of live multi-provider prices or cash reconciliation.
Q59: Propagate verified tenant/resource identity through uploads, storage metadata, ingest jobs, vector queries and graph predicates. Recheck current permissions/version before output and direct citation/download access. Namespaces and embeddings are derived data, not membership authority. Include cross-tenant, revoked-share, updated/deleted-source and delayed-result tests for every actual adapter; local SQL fixtures do not establish isolation in untested external services.
Q60: Define the claimed population and observation window: users, sessions, requests and concurrent work are different. Preserve original logs/monitoring and state missing evidence rather than borrowing a new synthetic benchmark. A defensible load result includes hardware, payload, traffic shape, warmup, errors and percentile latency. Availability also requires a denominator and failure window; a successful deployment or page load does not establish it.
